text:
Retrieval mass can reflect shortcuts rather than relevance. [DuoRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05730) documents representation degeneration in sequential recommendation; anisotropic embeddings can make unrelated histories appear similar. A [gradient analysis of popularity bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01154) finds popular items receive stronger positive gradients and different gradient directions. These findings motivate checking embedding cosine distributions, effective rank, and correlations between retrieval mass, item frequency, history length, and repeated-item counts before interpreting mass as confidence.

For nonnegative kernel weights, retrieval r=Σ(wᵢvᵢ)/(1+Σwᵢ) equals the weighted mean multiplied by S/(1+S), where S=Σwᵢ. This permits abstention at low mass, analogous to the null-value option proposed in [softmax₁](https://www.evanmiller.org/attention-is-off-by-one.html). However, duplicating interactions increases S even without new evidence; longer histories can therefore weaken shrinkage mechanically. This is an algebraic implication, not evidence of improved recommendation. [Sigmoid-attention research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04431) likewise emphasizes appropriate normalization and initialization.

Optimization risk: for residual αr with α=sigmoid(a), a very small initial α suppresses retrieval-branch gradients; sigmoid saturation also slows gate learning. Separately, [gradient starvation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.09468) explains how easily learned features can suppress learning of other predictive features. Suggested ablations: retrieval disabled; normalized mean versus mass shrinkage; deduplicated retrieval histories; cosine versus dot-product kernels; fixed versus learned residual scales. Track branch gradient norms, gate values, residual-to-backbone norms, and validation HR@10 by history length and target popularity. Use the prescribed four-category macro validation HR@10 for selection; these diagnostics do not establish causal user traits.
